newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asians want to attract savings back from the West.
newsitem.headline: Asians want to attract savings back from the West.

text.p: Asia's huge foreign exchange reserves are largely invested with developed countries despite the region's own need for investment funds, the head of Hong Kong's de facto central bank said on Friday.
Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), said the region needed to develop sophisticated markets and instruments to bring fund flows back home.
Five out of the top seven holders of foreign exchange reserves in the world were in Asia, he told an International Monetary Fund-HKMA conference here.

"And yet the process of financial intermediation in which the very substantial savings of this region are mobilised to satisfy the demand for investment funds, is, putting it mildly, a peculiar one," Yam said.
"Foreign reserves are predominantly invested in financial assets of developed economies rather than in the region," he said.
This meant policy makers had to deal with volatile capital flows and their impact on monetary stability, Yam said.
Yam said some people had "unkindly described this scenario as Asia providing funds for the hedge funds in New York to play havoc with Asian currencies and financial markets."
Rafael Hui, Hong Kong's Secretary for Financial Services, agreed, saying more than 95 percent of the territory's foreign reserves of about US$65 billion were invested outside Asia.
About 75 percent were invested in U.S. dollar assets, according to government figures.
Since 1983, the Hong Kong dollar has been pegged to the U.S. dollar, requiring the territory's financial authorities to invest heavily in high-quality U.S dollar assets to back up the peg.
"In sum, the overall picture seems to be that a significant portion of Asian savings have gone to OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development) markets," Hui said.
"In the other direction, there has been much foreign direct investment and foreign portfolio investment from OECD countries in Asia," Hui said.
Since channelling savings into investment was one important role of domestic financial systems, policy-makers and central bankers should perhaps question the phenomenon, Hui said.
Yam said Asia needed liquid financial markets with a greater variety of financial instruments, robust financial infrastructure and harmonised supervisory and regulatory standards.
